questions.explain: A 50ms query running 2M times/day does more bill damage than a 10-second query running hourly. Costs accumulate via three mechanisms: compute (CPU time forcing larger instance classes — e.g., r6g.2xlarge→4xlarge = +$382/mo), I/O (full scans driving provisioned-IOPS bills), and network/replication (huge result sets, binlog traffic at $0.01/GB cross-AZ).
options: Fast queries run millions of times cost more than slow rare ones — costs flow through compute (instance sizing), I/O (provisioned IOPS), and network/replication (large result sets, cross-AZ transfer)
questions.q: Why does the chapter distinguish 'slow' from 'expensive' queries, and what are the three cost mechanisms?

questions.explain: Three cost components per query: compute_cost_usd = total_cpu_seconds × (instance_cost_per_hour / vCPU_count / 3600); io_cost_usd = physical_reads × 8KB × storage rate (~$0.115/GB); est_monthly = (compute + I/O) scaled from the observation window to 30 days. SQL Server source: sys.dm_exec_query_stats (or Query Store), execution_count > 50, ordered by monthly estimate.
options: compute = CPU seconds × instance cost per vCPU-second; I/O = physical reads × storage rate; monthly = scaled to 30 days — sourced from sys.dm_exec_query_stats / Query Store

questions.explain: Combine Performance Insights (top SQL by db.load.avg grouped by db.sql.tokenized_id over 7 days) with Cost Explorer (total RDS cost for the same period): total DB cost ÷ total DB load = cost per AAS unit, enriching each SQL digest with dollar values. The daily pipeline (Lambda 06:00 UTC) writes dbo.query_cost_attribution and posts Slack alerts when a query exceeds the threshold (default $500/month).
options: Cost Explorer alone shows per-query cost
Manual review is the only option
Performance Insights top-SQL by DB load + Cost Explorer total cost → cost per AAS unit; daily pipeline writes dbo.query_cost_attribution with Slack alerts over $500/mo per query

questions.explain: Pattern 1: high disk blocks read + row efficiency below 0.10 (53 rows examined per row returned) → missing composite index (98% I/O reduction possible); pattern 2: chatty query — 28M calls at 0.3ms → batch with WHERE IN/TVP or cache. Pattern 3: high CPU, modest I/O aggregation → indexed views/pre-aggregation or read-replica offload; pattern 4: N+1 — call counts that are exact multiples (1,500 page queries → 45,000 lookups) → JOINs or ORM eager loading.
options: All patterns have the same fix

Low row efficiency → missing index; high call count + trivial cost → batch/cache; high CPU aggregation → indexed views/pre-aggregation; call counts in exact multiples → N+1, fix with JOINs/eager loading
questions.q: What are the four waste patterns in attribution output and their fixes?

questions.explain: The top 5% of queries account for 70–80% of database compute spend; fixing three to five of them typically cuts monthly bills by $2,000–$15,000 without touching infrastructure. A time-series of attribution snapshots catches regressions: week-over-week query comparing this week vs last week, flagging >20% cost increases (HIGH severity if the delta exceeds $200).
options: Top 5% of queries = 70–80% of compute spend; fixing 3–5 cuts $2,000–$15,000/mo; week-over-week trend analysis flags >20% cost growth before it hits the bill
